text.p: Poor interim earnings at Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd prompted some analysts to downgrade their 1997 forecasts on Thursday, with weak traffic and a strong U.S. dollar expected to continue hurting the Hong Kong carrier.
"The results were very disappointing and way below our expectations. I will be revising," said Merrill Lynch analyst Wendy Wong.
Cathay Pacific reported a 35 percent drop in earnings for the first six months of 1997 to HK$1.07 billion. Wong had been expecting first-half net profit of HK$1.12 billion.
Cathay said a suspension of its Airbus A330-300 service in late May due to engine problems, a slump in Japanese traffic and the strength of the U.S. dollar had hurt its performance.
Wong declined to say what her new forecast would be, but Merrill Lynch's previous full-year estimate was net profit of HK$3.7 billion compared with HK$3.81 billion posted in 1996.
Percy Au-Young, director of research at DBS Securities, said he had expected interim net profit of HK$1.2 billion.
"I assumed they were able to recoup all losses incurred from the Airbus engine problems but it seems to me that may be there is some net loss from that," he said.
Cathay Pacific said its first-half results included compensation from Rolls-Royce Plc for losses linked to problems with its Rolls Royce Trent 700 powered Airbus fleet.
Au-Young revised his full-year net profit estimate to HK$3.25 billion from a previous estimate of HK$3.56 billion.

John Hetherington, an analyst at Paribas Asia Equity, said he had expected first-half net profit of HK$1.2 billion and would now revise his full-year net profit forecast to HK$3.3 billion from a previous estimate of HK$3.4 billion.
"There are certain factors that won't change in the second half," Hetherington said.
"You have got a U.S. dollar which is still very strong and that is certainly hurting them on the yield side. So the inclination is that you will see more yield pressure," he said.
Cathay said on Wednesday that downward pressure on yields and the weakness of certain European currencies had reduced revenues on many routes in the first half.

Recent currency turmoil in Asia would also have an impact, analysts said. "Reporting earnings in a regional currency which is still comfortably tied to the U.S. dollar CX (Cathay) will be severely challenged to increase its ASEAN derived profits this year," Hetherington said in a recent research report.
Wong said she did not expect to see a pick up in traffic numbers during the second half. "Traffic numbers continue to be weak and we do not anticipate a pickup," she said.

Cathay Pacific said a summer traffic peak around the period of Hong Kong's return to Chinese rule on July 1 had failed to materialise and the Japanese market, which is an important market for Cathay Pacific, had seen a considerable decline in visitors to Hong Kong.
"The second half of the year traditionally brings a strong demand for air travel, although there is still a hesitation in some markets to visit Hong Kong," Cathay said on Wednesday.
Both Hetherington and Wong were negative on the stock.
Cathay Pacific shares fell HK$0.55, or 3.93 percent, to close at HK$13.45 at midsession on Thursday.
"The stock has come off quite a bit and may have a little further to go," said Wong.
